sources.news_title: Doug Ford's blunt warning to Trump over Canada tariffs
sources.text:
Watch: Doug Ford's blunt warning to Trump over Canada tariffs
Ontario Premier Doug Ford has warned US President Donald Trump that Canada can hit back against tariffs to hurt the American economy.
Listing some of the industries he said the US relies on, Ford said: "I'd love to see him run cars without any oil. I'd love to see him to try grow vegetables and fruit without the potash."
Highlighting the anger felt in Canada over the trade dispute, the blunt speaking Ford also doubled down on his taunt to the US president.

sources.news_title: Canadian leaders won’t rule out using energy, critical minerals as retaliation against U.S.
sources.text:
Prime Minister Mark Carney and at least two premiers won’t rule out targeting energy and critical minerals as Canada weighs going beyond the dollar-for-dollar counter-tariffs already announced in response to 50 per cent U.S. duties on roughly $28 billion of Canadian goods.
The U.S. tariffs exclude energy, potash and some critical minerals, underscoring their importance to American industry.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford said Monday that “everything’s on the table,” including electricity and critical minerals, but that any escalation should be coordinated with Ottawa and the other provinces. That marks a shift for Ford, whose province acted on its own last fall when it ran a U.S. television ad using Ronald Reagan’s words against tariffs, a move that prompted Trump to break off trade talks.
“I can’t do this alone, folks. I need every premier playing on Team Canada, and I’m confident that every single premier will be part of Team Canada,” Ford told reporters. “No matter if it’s our electricity that we ship down there, but many other provinces’ electricity, and other areas that we can really put pain on the U.S. no matter if it’s the oil or if it’s potash or if it’s uranium.”
Ford imposed a 25 per cent surcharge on electricity exports to Michigan, Minnesota and New York last March, then dropped it after a single day when Trump threatened to double tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum. On Monday he said Ontario could raise power prices again.
“That electricity surcharge is gonna be on the table,” Ford said, though he added that he would hold off for now. “I don’t want to escalate it anymore, but we need to fight back.”
Last year, Canada sent 35 terawatt-hours of electricity to the U.S., representing less than two per cent of total U.S. electricity generation and adding $3.4 billion to the Canadian economy, according to RBC.
But some states are more dependent on Canadian power than others.
Ontario supplies six per cent of Michigan’s electricity needs, much of it is pushed out to neighbouring states, mainly Ohio and Indiana. New York, meanwhile, is reliant on Quebec and Ontario for six per cent of its power.
Ford said the retaliation should target Republican-held states where economic pressure could have political consequences ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.
RBC’s head of climate research, Myha Truong-Regan, writes that Ontario and Quebec would need to have a coordinated strategy “if electricity is going to be an effective bargaining chip with the U.S. administration.”
READ MORE: Canada vows dollar-for-dollar tariff retaliation, suspends trade talks with U.S.
Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette said that Canada should respond by hitting “where there’s sensitivity” while adding she had not yet considered the measures Ford is proposing.
“But nothing’s excluded because this is a new phase that we’re entering now,” she said.
Quebec has less room to manoeuvre, as Hydro-Québec has supplied New York for more than a century and is locked into a 20-year contract to deliver up to 900 megawatts to the state’s grid operator through 2030, which may limit its ability to add surcharges or curtail exports.
Québec solidaire, campaigning in the provincial election, said it would raise Hydro-Québec’s export rates to pressure Washington, part of a tariff-response plan unveiled by party leader Ruba Ghazal on Monday.
Carney insists Canada has leverage
Meanwhile, Prime Minister Mark Carney travelled to Lévis, Que., to announce an $11-billion shipbuilding contract with Davie, repeatedly framing the deal as a reminder of “the many things the United States needs from Canada.”
He quipped that the U.S. has “a handful, and I’m being generous” of icebreakers to Canada’s 20, with the expertise to build more concentrated here.
Asked about retaliation, Carney said the initial focus should be on building the economy, but rejected Trump’s claim that the U.S. needs nothing from Canada.
“We provide them with energy. We provide them with critical minerals. We provide them with key products in their supply chains for the automotive industry and other industries,” he said.
“So we’re staying calm. We’ll stay positive… And yes, if we need to do more, well, we’ll see.”
Posting to Truth Social on Monday afternoon, U.S. President Donald Trump repeated his frequent claim that Canada could not survive without the U.S. and wrote, in part, “much of the Electricity, Oil, and Gas that Canada gets is transported through the U.S.A. Someone should get these clowns to “fall in line” or, the consequences for Canada will be far WORSE!”
Some Western Canadian crude does reach Ontario and Quebec through pipelines that cross the U.S., such as Enbridge’s Line 5, which carries more than half a million barrels of crude oil and natural gas liquids daily from Superior, Wis., through Michigan to Sarnia, Ont.
Canada supplied about 63 per cent of U.S. crude oil imports in 2025 and nearly all of its imported natural gas, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
But oil-rich Alberta has no interest in seeing its energy used as a weapon, with Premier Danielle Smith saying earlier in July that withholding energy exports is “not going to happen,” and warning again on Saturday that retaliation would be costly.
“I know emotionally it feels good to retaliate, I get that,” she said on her radio show. “But when retaliation happens, it means that everybody who is buying products from the United States is now going to face upwards to 50 per cent tariffs.”
Not everyone in the province agrees. In an open letter to constituents Monday, Airdrie-Cochrane MLA Peter Guthrie, leader of the Progressive Tory Party of Alberta, accused Smith of weakening Canada’s position.
“You don’t have to use every lever available,” he wrote, “but you certainly don’t surrender your leverage in advance.”
Ford hopes critical minerals could provide another source of leverage. He said Ontario supplies high-grade nickel used by the U.S. military and manufacturing sectors and suggested restricting access to such resources could form part of Canada’s response if the dispute escalates.
He said that measures involving electricity, fuel, potash, uranium and other strategically important exports would be most effective if provinces and Ottawa move together.
“A couple premiers have a lot of power to protect Canada — massive power,” Ford said. “I can’t speak for them, but we need everyone to be on Team Canada and throw everything and the kitchen sink at them.”

sources.news_title: Carney says Trump’s demands would dismantle Canadian auto industry as Ontario Premier warns US could be cut off
Canada says Trump tariffs aim to break its auto industry
sources.text:
Canada says Trump tariffs aim to break its auto industry
Mark Carney said fresh US trade demands and threatened tariffs target Canada's auto industry. Ontario warned it could curb electricity and critical minerals, deepening a sovereignty-driven standoff.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Monday that fresh US trade demands had confirmed Canada's fears that President Donald Trump was trying to break its auto industry, as Trump threatened new 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian vehicles, auto parts and steel from next year. Carney said Canada was still willing to negotiate, but only if Washington treated the talks as a partnership between sovereign countries.
The dispute escalated as Ontario Premier Doug Ford warned that Canada could respond by cutting off electricity and critical minerals to the United States. Ford said Trump had misread Canada's resolve, while Carney said US proposals for the auto sector would "gradually dismantle" Canadian production and damage a deeply integrated industry on both sides of the border.
Carney said that "an attitude at the negotiation table that Canada is a subsidiary of the United States" was "not something we're going to accept". He added that Canada is the biggest customer for US automobiles and questioned what Trump's latest move would mean for workers in states such as Ohio, Kentucky and Alabama who depend on Canadian demand. "This is the most successful automotive partnership in history," Carney said.
Trump said on social media that Canada had been "ripping off the United States of America for years" and criticised what he called Canada's "ridiculously high tariffs" on American farmers. Carney had walked away from trade negotiations with the Trump administration late on Friday, saying Washington wanted too much in return for tariff relief. The United States imposed 50 per cent tariffs on about USD 20 billion worth of Canadian goods on Saturday, and Carney announced dollar-for-dollar retaliation from September 8.
In an interview with The Associated Press, Ford said Trump had "declared war, economic war against his closest friend and ally" and had underestimated Canadians' willingness to bear economic pain rather than yield to pressure. "He underestimates Canada. We're all in," Ford said. "Up here, we're at a fever pitch, everyone's in for an economic war. They know they're going to have to sacrifice." Ford, a Progressive Conservative, comes from a different party than Carney, a Liberal, underscoring the wider political unity in Canada over the dispute.
Ford said "everything is on the table" if the standoff worsened, including stopping supplies of electricity and critical minerals from Ontario. "I'll cut them off," he said of critical minerals. "You won't get a grain of sand out of Ontario." He specifically pointed to high-grade nickel sent to the United States and uranium refined in Ontario, and said Canada should also consider using oil and potash as leverage. "We power 1.5 million homes and businesses," Ford said. "Everything's on the table. I'll do whatever it takes." He added that if Trump kept trying to dismantle Canadian manufacturing, "he better have a pack of batteries."
Critical minerals have become increasingly important for US national security and manufacturing. The Pentagon has been seeking more secure supplies of minerals used in military aircraft, missiles, munitions and electronics as Washington tries to reduce reliance on China, which dominates the mining or processing of several strategically important minerals.
Ford said Trump was not simply trying to secure a better trade deal, but was aiming to hollow out Canadian industries and shift production south. "He wants to bleed out every single sector and bring them down to the US," Ford said, adding that Trump wanted to make Canada a "vassal state". Ontario is the centre of Canada's vehicle manufacturing industry, and its plants and suppliers are closely linked with factories in Michigan and other US states, with parts often crossing the border several times during production. Automakers including Ford, General Motors and Stellantis have major assembly plants in Ontario, and the supply chain supports tens of thousands of jobs.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said on Monday that "the only reason Canada has auto production in the first place" was the 1960s Auto Pact, under which Canada used access to its market to encourage vehicle production north of the border. Ford rejected that argument, saying, "If he thinks the Canadian people are going to roll over and just continue buying American-made vehicles, it's not going to happen."
Ford also said he had opposed the preliminary agreement that Carney had been considering before Canada stepped away from the negotiations. "I wasn't supporting the deal," he said. He added that he was unwilling to restore American liquor to Ontario store shelves as part of any agreement and was prepared to publicly break with it. "I wasn't going to put the booze back on the shelves," Ford said. "I was ready to go out there and call a press conference ... and say I'm not buckling over." Ford said he understood that Washington had also sought language late in the talks that would have limited Canada's ability to negotiate trade deals with other countries without US approval. Carney has called that demand unacceptable and a matter of Canadian sovereignty. "Who does he think he is?" Ford said of Trump. "You gotta be kidding."
Ford's criticism of Trump also revived his earlier invocation of former US President Ronald Reagan. Ford noted that Trump keeps a portrait of Reagan near his desk and said, "He'd be throwing up on him from the picture if he knew what was going on, spinning around in his grave right now. He should maybe take that picture off the wall and move it somewhere else. Because right now, Ronald Reagan would be disgusted with President Trump." The White House responded by saying Reagan had taken similar action against Japan. Spokesman Kush Desai said, "President Reagan enacted a 100% tariff on Japanese electronics for dumping on the US market and failing to open up Japan's market to Made-in-USA goods." Ford's Reagan remarks recalled a previous clash with Trump after Ontario paid for US television advertisements featuring a 1987 Reagan speech warning that tariffs could trigger retaliation and trade wars. Trump had accused Ontario of misrepresenting Reagan and halted trade talks with Canada, before Ford later agreed to pause the campaign so talks could resume.
Even as the rhetoric hardened, Ford said Canada should continue engaging with Washington. "I never believe in walking away from the table," he said. "Continue negotiating and see where we go." The latest exchange left Canada and the United States facing a sharper trade confrontation, with the auto sector at its centre and both sides warning of wider consequences.
With PTI Inputs

sources.news_title: CP U.S. should feel pain in tariff war, Ontario Premier Doug Ford says
sources.text:
The United States needs to feel the pain in response to Donald Trump's latest tariff war escalation, Ontario Premier Doug Ford said Monday as he and the president traded insults.
Ford had earlier said on Toronto radio that Trump should "kiss my ass" after the president threatened further tariffs on the auto and steel sectors that could come into play on Jan. 1, 2027.
Ford doubled down at a news conference in Hamilton.
"I have a lot of real estate on my ass, so he has a lot a room to kiss my ass," Ford said with a smile.
Ford said he was against last week's proposed trade deal before the Canada-U.S. negotiations fell apart and called for a strong response to new 50 per cent tariffs on $28 billion of Canadian exports. He said Prime Minister Mark Carney has his full support.
"We'll see how this goes, but he wants to put pain on Canadians," Ford said of Trump. "We'll leverage every bit of pain we possibly can on Americans."
He said everything is on the table, including cutting off Ontario's electricity and critical minerals supplies to the United States.
The premier's comments caught Trump's attention.
"Lots of 'bluster' from Doug Ford, who is the Premier of the Canadian Province of Ontario, but who is better known as the less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive brother of the late, great Rob Ford," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.
In response, Ford said: "the guy's a loser."
Ford weighed in on the trade war after remaining quiet for several days while talks between the two countries intensified, until breaking off just before new tariffs took effect on Saturday.
Carney suspended the trade talks on Friday night, accusing the Trump administration of introducing unacceptable measures including restrictions on Canada's ability to sign deals with other countries and last-minute demands to restrict Canada's language and culture protections.
Ford applauded Carney's decision to walk away from the deal and called for the country's premiers to stand united.
Ottawa plans to match U.S. tariffs dollar-for-dollar after Labour Day, targeting sectors including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment and electronics.
Ford said he is considering another surcharge on electricity Ontario sends to 1.5 million customers in Michigan, New York and Minnesota.
When Trump went ahead with his original tariffs against Canada last year, Ford retaliated by implementing a 25 per cent surcharge on electricity to those states. The Trump administration was livid and threatened increased tariffs. But the gambit spurred renewed trade talks and Ontario's surcharge only lasted a day.
Ford also mused about cutting off electricity altogether to those states.
Trump, meanwhile, launched his own energy threat on Monday.
"Remember, much of the electricity, oil and gas that Canada gets is transported through the U.S.A.," he wrote. "Someone should get these clowns to 'fall in line' or the consequences for Canada will be far WORSE!"
Ford also pulled American booze off the shelves of the Liquor Control Board of Ontario in March 2025 in retaliation to Trumps' first volley of tariffs.
That move effectively banned bourbon, California wines and a host of other U.S. liquor, wine and ready-to-drink beverages across the province.
Ford has said he would drop the booze ban once Trump drops all tariffs he has imposed on Canada.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 24, 2026.
Liam Casey and Maan Alhmidi, The Canadian Press

Trump announced the new tariff threat on Truth Social after trade talks between the U.S. and Canada collapsed over the weekend. In a separate interview with the Associated Press, Ford vowed to cut off electricity and critical minerals from Ontario to the U.S.
Ontario’s leader said electricity exported by Canada powers 1.5 million homes and businesses across certain U.S. states, including Michigan, Minnesota, and New York. Canada’s critical minerals are vital to America’s national security and defense manufacturing.

Reagan would “be throwing up on him from the picture [displayed in the Oval Office] if he knew what was going on, spinning around in his grave right now,” Ford told the Associated Press. “He should maybe take that picture off the wall and move it somewhere else. Because right now, Ronald Reagan would be disgusted with President Trump.”

Ontario Premier Doug Ford’s threat to cut off electricity and critical minerals to the United States has sparked a response from President Donald Trump, who is accusing both Ford and Prime Minister Mark Carney of “bad leadership.”
Trump warned about cutting off pipelines and electrical lines carrying energy to Canada in the face of Ford’s threat.

Ontario’s anti-tariff ads in the United States in 2025 also became a point of contention with Trump, who abruptly ended trade talks with Canada over the ads.

sources.news_title: Trump vs. Doug Ford feud timeline amid US-Canada trade dispute
sources.text:
Canada's Ontario Premier Doug Ford said former U.S. President Ronald Reagan would be "throwing up" over the trade policies of President Donald Trump. It is just the latest in a series of comments from Ford speaking out against Trump and his policies.
In an interview with The Associated Press, Ford said Trump keeps a portrait of Reagan—a consistently popular Republican president who championed free trade—near his desk, but that the late leader would be "disgusted with President Trump."
Referring to Trump's tariffs and interventionist measures, which he says are at odds with Reagan's economic policies, Ford added, "[Reagan would] be throwing up on him from the picture if he knew what was going on."
Ford's comments on Monday came after trade talks between the U.S. and Canada broke down, with Ottawa retaliating after Trump slapped 50 percent tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods.
Ford, who has served as premier of the most populous Canadian province since 2018, has repeatedly taken swipes since Trump returned to the Oval Office, although he previously told Politico he would “absolutely” get along with the U.S. president and wanted good ties with the U.S. The U.S. president has directed criticism at Ford and, more broadly, at Ontario.
Newsweek has reached out to the White House and Ford’s office.
What Ford Has Said About Trump
January 6, 2025: Trump's threats to impose 25 percent tariffs on products from Canada and rhetoric about wanting to make the country the 51st state prompted mockery from Ford, who said, “I’ll make him a counteroffer, how about if we buy Alaska, and we'll throw in Minnesota and Minneapolis at the same time.”
Minnesota shares a 550-mile border with Canada about 320 miles of which is shared with Ontario.
Ford went on to say Trump was "joking” and that a merger between the countries was "not realistic” as he noted the critical minerals, oil and electricity Canada sends to the U.S.
“These are all areas and different sectors that Americans need and why disrupt that.”
January 22, 2025: In the Politico interview, Ford said, “I’m a street fighter in politics,” adding that, “if someone throws a punch at me, I’m going to hit him back twice as hard.”
Ford said that Trump’s targeting of Canada in a trade war could lead to the premier cutting power transmission to U.S. homes and businesses and banning U.S. liquor from Ontario shelves. He pledged to target red states with dollar-for-dollar retaliation.
However, Ford said that he did not want to make these moves, telling the outlet, “I want to work with President Trump.”
February 27, 2025: After Ford claimed a third straight victory for his Progressive Conservatives in the province's election, he said he had been given a "mandate" to "stand up" to Trump’s tariff threats, adding, "Let me be clear. Canada will never, ever be the 51st state.”
March 4, 2025: Canadian media reported that Ford blamed Trump for "causing chaos" with tariff threats.
Ford criticized Trump and called on U.S. Republican politicians to push back, saying that the U.S. president “needs to pay the price in the midterms," adding, “If I've got to go down there and knock on the doors myself, I will."
March 10, 2025: Ford announced that Ontario would charge 25 percent more for electricity to 1.5 million American homes and businesses in response to Trump’s trade war. Minnesota receives some of its electricity from the Canadian province.
“I will not hesitate to increase this charge. If the United States escalates, I will not hesitate to shut the electricity off completely,” Ford told a news conference in Toronto.
March 26, 2025: Ford mocked Trump’s framing of tariffs as “Liberation Day," days before the U.S. leader announced them on April 2.
“I know President Trump likes telling people, ‘you’re fired.’ I didn’t think he meant auto workers in the U.S.” Ford told a news conference, referring to Trump’s catchphrase on the reality TV show The Apprentice. Ford called the policy, “Termination Day for American workers."
April 24, 2025: During the Canada Growth Summit, Ford accused Trump of wanting to destroy Canadian auto and manufacturing, saying, “I think the cheese slips off the cracker with this guy."
“He wakes up in the morning and even people around him are not too sure what he’s going to do,” Ford added.
August 7, 2025: During an interview with CNN, Ford responded to a question about how Canadians view Trump after tariffs and threats of the country becoming the 51st state.
“He’s probably the most disliked politician in the world in Canada because he’s attacked his closest family member.”
September 29, 2025: After Trump announced new trade measures targeting the global film industry, including a 100 percent tariff on all movies produced outside the U.S., Ford told reporters, “I disagree with anything that guy says. He drives me crazy.”
July 20, 2026: Trump threatened tariffs if Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney didn’t address wildfire smoke coming into the U.S. from Canada, saying it was caused by negligence in forest management and debris removal.
In a news conference, Ford responded, saying, “With all the assets the U.S. has, and he’s sitting there complaining. Why don’t you send up some water bombers? Why don’t you start helping us?”
July 24, 2026: During an interview with CBS News, Ford accused Trump of economically attacking Canada, saying, “When someone comes up and punches you in the face, not once, not twice, 10 times, you have to stand up to that person.”
August 13, 2026: Ford teased the development of data centers in the province, telling an audience in Guelph, “Either we do it, or Donald Trump’s going to do it. And I’m not giving Donald Trump nothing, absolutely nothing.”
August 22, 2026: In his first public comments since the trade spat saw Canada retaliate against Trump's tariffs, Ford said that the U.S. president "is the type of person that would steal your lunch money the first day,” adding, “He'd steal the toque off your head the second day and the third day he'd steal your running shoes.”
“He is not to be trusted whatsoever. We need to stay united,” Ford added.
August 24, 2026: Speaking to reporters, Ford responded to Trump's latest tariff threat, saying, "I don't respond to a dictator like President Trump, a bully like President Trump... I'm not gonna take any advice off a guy that's the king of bankruptcies. He's actually tariffing his own people, taxing his own people."
He added that he had a message for American voters ahead of the midterms, saying Trump had not delivered on his promises of lower costs.
Trump’s Responses To Ford and Comments About Ontario and Canada
March 10, 2025: Trump, on Truth Social, responded to a move by Ford to impose a 25 percent surcharge on electricity flowing to three U.S. states, writing, “Canada is a tariff abuser, and always has been, but the United States is not going to be subsidizing Canada any longer.”
Trump continued, saying, Canada "will pay a financial price for this so big that it will be read about in History Books for many years to come!"
March 11, 2025: Trump had words of praise for Ford after he suspended the electricity surcharge for U.S. customers, calling him a “very strong man in Canada” although he suggested that it was pressure from the White House that led to the move.
“We had a problem with Ontario and they dropped that,” Trump said. “We let them know what we were going to be doing, they dropped it immediately.”
October 16, 2025: Trump terminated trade talks and imposed an additional 10 percent levy on Canadian goods after Ford’s team launched a U.S. campaign highlighting comments from Reagan that tariffs hurt workers and trigger trade wars.
The clips were from an address delivered by Reagan on April 25, 1987, and while the ad didn’t change any of the GOP president's words, it condensed his comments in a way that The Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation and Institute said misrepresented Reagan’s views.
Trump did not mention Ford directly, but responded on Truth Social.
"Canada has fraudulently used an advertisement, which is FAKE, featuring Ronald Reagan speaking negatively about Tariffs."
August 23, 2026: After trade talks collapsed and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced reciprocal tariffs, Trump posted on Truth Social, “Canada wants the benefits of being a State, without being one.”
“They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of Tariffs. No more!!!” the post added.
August 24, 2026: After earlier announcing increased tariffs, Trump posted again on Truth Social, saying, "Lots of “bluster” from Doug Ford, who is the Premier of the Canadian Province of Ontario, but who is better known as the less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive brother of the late, great, Rob Ford."
The president went on to claim the U.S. "will always" be bigger, richer, and stronger than Canada. He also said the country would not be able to continue taking advantage of the U.S., "because of their current bad leadership, primarily Governor Carney, and his Flunky, Ford."
Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Daniel Orton, Dan Gooding and Geoffrey Rowland.

sources.news_title: ‘We’re All In’: Ontario Premier Warns Trump Canada Is Ready to Cut Off Electricity and Critical Minerals to the U.S. Over His Trade War
sources.text:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford has a message for Donald Trump: Canada isn’t backing down.
In an interview with The Associated Press, Ford said Canada should be prepared to use some of its most valuable resources as leverage if Trump’s escalating trade war gets worse — including electricity and critical minerals that the United States relies on.
“He underestimates Canada. We’re all in,” Ford said.
And according to Ford, Canadians are ready to absorb some economic pain rather than surrender to Trump’s demands.
“Up here, we’re at a fever pitch, everyone’s in for an economic war. They know they’re going to have to sacrifice.”
That’s a striking escalation from the leader of Canada’s most populous province.
Ford has previously warned that Ontario could cut off electricity exports to the United States almost instantly. Now he’s saying critical minerals, oil and potash could also become bargaining chips.
In other words: if Trump wants a trade war, Canada is preparing to fight back with the things America needs.
## “He declared war”
Ford didn’t mince words when describing Trump’s trade policies.
He said Trump has effectively “declared war, economic war against his closest friend and ally.”
And Ford wasn’t finished.
He brought Ronald Reagan into the fight.
Trump keeps a portrait of Reagan near his desk, but Ford argued that the former Republican president would be horrified by Trump’s protectionist trade policies.
Reagan was a strong advocate of free trade and repeatedly warned about the dangers of tariffs and retaliation.
“He’d be throwing up on him from the picture if he knew what was going on, spinning around in his grave right now,” Ford said.
Ford went on to suggest Trump should take Reagan’s picture off the wall.
“Because right now, Ronald Reagan would be disgusted with President Trump.”
That’s a remarkable attack coming from the leader of a major Canadian province — and one that echoes a fight Ford has already had with Trump over trade.
## Canada walks away, Trump escalates
Ford’s comments came after Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney walked away from trade negotiations with the Trump administration late Friday.
Carney said Washington was demanding too much in exchange for tariff relief.
The United States then imposed 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion worth of Canadian goods, while Carney announced dollar-for-dollar retaliation beginning September 8.
Trump escalated the confrontation again Monday, threatening a 50% tariff on Canadian automobiles, auto parts and steel beginning next year.
“Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years,” Trump wrote on social media.
He also complained about what he called Canada’s “ridiculously high tariffs” on American farmers.
“Not sustainable, and NOT ANYMORE!” Trump declared.
Ford’s response was essentially: bring it on.
Ford said “everything is on the table” if the dispute gets worse. That includes electricity.
It also includes critical minerals that are increasingly important to American manufacturing and national security.
“I’ll cut them off,” Ford said of critical minerals.
“You won’t get a grain of sand out of Ontario.”
Ford specifically pointed to high-grade nickel shipped to the United States and uranium refined in Ontario.
“What would they do without the high-grade nickel that we ship down to the U.S.?” he asked.
That’s not an insignificant question.
Critical minerals are used in everything from electronics to military equipment, including aircraft, missiles and munitions. The United States has been trying to secure more reliable supplies and reduce its dependence on China.
Ford also suggested Canada could use oil and potash as additional leverage.
And then there’s electricity.
Ontario supplies power to 1.5 million homes and businesses in the United States, according to Ford.
“Everything’s on the table. I’ll do whatever it takes,” he said.
Ford has used electricity as a weapon in the trade fight before.
During an earlier escalation, Ontario imposed a 25% surcharge on electricity exported to Michigan, Minnesota and New York.
Trump responded by threatening to double tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum.
Eventually, both sides backed away.
This time, Ford sounds far less interested in backing down.
“If Trump continues trying to dismantle Canadian manufacturing,” Ford warned, “he better have a pack of batteries.”
The auto industry may be the biggest battleground of all.
Ontario is the heart of Canada’s vehicle manufacturing industry, with major plants operated by Ford, General Motors and Stellantis.
The supply chain is deeply integrated with the United States. Auto parts routinely cross the border multiple times before a vehicle is completed.
That means a major tariff fight could hit manufacturers and workers on both sides of the border.
Ford believes that’s exactly what Trump wants.
He accused the president of trying to hollow out Canadian industries and move production south.
“He wants to bleed out every single sector and bring them down to the U.S.,” Ford said.
Ford went even further, accusing Trump of wanting to turn Canada into a “vassal state.”
The Trump administration sees it differently.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer argued Monday that Canada’s auto industry exists in large part because of the 1960s Auto Pact, which used access to Canada’s market to encourage vehicle production north of the border.
Ford isn’t buying it.
“If he thinks the Canadian people are going to roll over and just continue buying American-made vehicles, it’s not going to happen,” he said.
## Ford says he was ready to blow up the deal
Ford also revealed that he opposed a preliminary agreement that Canadian negotiators were considering before Carney walked away from the talks.
“I wasn’t supporting the deal,” Ford said.
One sticking point was American liquor.
Ford said he wasn’t willing to put American alcohol back on Ontario store shelves as part of a trade agreement.
“I wasn’t going to put the booze back on the shelves,” he said. “I was ready to go out there and call a press conference … and say I’m not buckling over.”
But the bigger issue was sovereignty.
According to Ford, Washington sought language that would have restricted Canada’s ability to negotiate trade agreements with other countries without U.S. approval.
Carney has called that demand unacceptable.
Ford’s response was blunt: “Who does he think he is? You gotta be kidding.”
Ford’s latest comments also revive an earlier battle with Trump.
Last year, Ontario paid for television advertisements in the United States featuring excerpts from a 1987 Reagan speech warning about tariffs, retaliation and trade wars.
Trump accused Ford of misrepresenting Reagan and abruptly ended trade negotiations with Canada.
Ford eventually agreed to pause the advertising campaign so negotiations could resume.
Now Ford is once again invoking Reagan against Trump.
“He doesn’t respect anyone,” Ford said.
And yet, despite all the escalating rhetoric, Ford says he doesn’t want the two countries to stop talking.
“I never believe in walking away from the table,” he said.
“Continue negotiating and see where we go.”
That’s the strange reality of this increasingly ugly trade war.
Canada is threatening to cut off electricity, critical minerals and other resources.
Trump is threatening massive tariffs on Canadian industries.
For Ford, that’s apparently where the line is: Canada is willing to fight — but it’s still willing to talk.

“Look, at the end of the day, I do think that Doug Ford talks really tough, in moments like this, but we haven't seen real action.”

“It's working people right now that are suffering. They just cannot afford even the basics already. So yes, life is going to get tougher, and we should retaliate with everything we've got. But let's not pretend … that's all it's going to take,” she said.

“This is not WWE Smackdown, right? It's not who's going to get the biggest insult in,” Fraser said. “That's not going to feed families. That's not going to protect jobs.”

TORONTO (AP) — The United States and Canada, historic allies along an undefended border, fell deeper into a trade war Saturday marked by angry recriminations and new tariffs that are expected to raise prices for products in both countries.
Each side blamed the other for the collapse of negotiations in Washington late Friday, leading the U.S. to impose 50% tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods and Canada setting Sept. 8 as the start of its retaliatory penalties.
President Donald Trump’s import taxes will hit about 5% of what Canada ships to the United States every year, ranging from hockey sticks to tongue depressors. Prime Minister Carney said Ottawa would respond with targeted tariff protection for industries exposed to the new U.S. duties, including some steel products. He also mentioned the dairy, appliance, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics sectors.
No further talks were planned. Whatever the eventual outcome, a loss of trust seems one of the earliest casualties.
Carney accused Washington of using “economic integration as a weapon” and said “its signature was written in pencil.” Resorting to the language of battle, he said his country had been “attacked” by the new American tariffs. “You’re at war when you get attacked,” he said, adding that Canada had the reserves, resilience and plan to respond.
But to Trump’s chief trade negotiator, Jamieson Greer, the U.S. was compelled to act after a year of retaliation by its longtime partner.
“We’ve said enough, and so we’ve taken countermeasures. Our interest is in protecting American workers and protecting American supply chains,” the U.S. trade representative told “Fox & Friends Weekend.”
Canada cites ‘unacceptable demands’ as US says it offered favorable terms
Carney said Canada had been willing to drop remaining retaliatory tariffs on steel, aluminum and autos if the U.S. substantially lowered its own, and to encourage provinces to restore U.S. alcohol sales. But he said Washington’s final demands went too far. “They asked too much and offered too little,” Carney said.
Greer said the Republican administration was offering to cut tariffs on steel, autos and lumber, “things that are sensitive for them. And they’ve always had the best deal, and they still would have an even better deal, but they didn’t want that.”
As a result, he said, “We’re moving forward with measures that respond to Canadian retaliation.”
Carney said the U.S. added last-minute terms that would have reduced tariff relief for Canadian-made vehicles, restricted Canada’s ability to strike trade deals with other countries and weakened protections for language, culture and sovereignty.
He said such demands were “unacceptable.”
The breakdown in negotiations marked a sharp reversal from two days earlier, when officials from the two countries sounded as if they were headed toward a compromise.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford, who leads Canada’s most populous province, praised Carney for rejecting the deal, saying it would have hurt Ontario’s auto, steel and manufacturing sectors. Ford urged Canada to use “every tool in our toolbox” to fight the U.S. tariffs.
The moves also call into question the future of a North American trade agreement covering the United States, Canada and Mexico that is crucial to industry in all three countries.
Carney said the breakdown was “certainly not good news” for the review of that agreement and that the failed negotiations had given Canada “a new perspective” on what Washington wants from the broader economic relationship.
A typically cooperative alliance goes sour
The political impact will likely be even bigger than the economic fallout. The countries sold each other $880 billion worth of goods and services last year.
The tariffs were initially supposed to kick in at 12:01 a.m. Wednesday. Trump extended the deadline for three days to allow talks to continue, but the countries could not reach an agreement in time.
The U.S. and Canada have wrangled for decades over trade, poking each other over sore spots such as Canadian softwood lumber imports and U.S. access to Canada’s protected dairy market.
Somehow, they still managed to remain friends, allies and trading partners. Canadian soldiers fought alongside Americans in Afghanistan after 9/11. The 5,525-mile U.S.-Canada border is undefended, and nearly 330,000 people and $2 billion worth of goods cross it every day; 800,000 Canadians live in the United States.
Trump’s approach to dealing with Canada marks an extraordinary departure from the traditionally cooperative relationship between the two countries. Trump has imposed tariffs on Canadian goods in a push to bring manufacturing back to the United States and made inflammatory comments about turning Canada into America’s 51st state.
Carney said Canada had recognized that “America has changed” and that the two countries would “not return to our old relationship.”
Canadians and Americans are frustrated
The Canadian public is fed up. A petition to expel U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra, a Trump ally, has collected nearly 248,000 signatures since July 21. It accuses the former Republican congressman from Michigan of having “normalized’’ Trump’s talk of annexing Canada, among other things.
The two countries had good reasons to find a compromise.
Nearly 72% of Canada’s goods exports last year went to the United States. The Trump administration might be wary of imposing new tariffs — paid by U.S. importers who try to pass along the cost to consumers via higher prices — before the November midterm elections. American voters are already frustrated with the high cost of living.
“Both sides will be under immense pressure in the coming days to still find an off-ramp,” said Ryan Majerus, a partner at King & Spalding and a former U.S. trade official.
Joshua Bolten, CEO of the Business Roundtable, which represents leaders of major U.S. companies, warned the tariffs and retaliation risk “raising costs for American businesses and families” and disrupting vital supply chains, and urged both governments to resume negotiations.
Trump has turned to Depression-era trade penalties
Trump has made tariffs the centerpiece of his second-term economic agenda. Last year, he imposed double-digit import taxes on almost every country, justifying them by declaring the long-standing U.S. trade deficit a national emergency. The Supreme Court in February ruled that he had overstepped his authority. The justices struck down the trade penalties and set the stage for the federal government to pay refunds to importers.
So Trump has looked for other legal authority to justify tariffs.
After the Supreme Court struck down much of Trump’s earlier tariff program in February, the administration turned to other legal authorities. For Canada, Trump invoked Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, a rarely used Depression-era provision allowing tariffs of up to 50% against countries deemed to discriminate against U.S. businesses.
The provision is part of the Smoot-Hawley tariff law, widely blamed by economists and historians for worsening the Great Depression by restricting global trade. Section 338 has never previously been used to impose tariffs.
The rift comes as the United States, Mexico and Canada are trying to renew a trade agreement that Trump negotiated in his first term and once praised as a triumph. The United States has begun formal talks with Mexico over revamping the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement, known as USMCA. But talks with Canada have not begun and escalating trade conflict casts doubt on whether they will.

Over the course of a 45-minute news conference, Ford repeatedly took aim at Trump, who he said could “kiss my ass.”
“Let’s be clear, I don’t like the guy — simple,” Ford told reporters.
Premier resists calls to recall legislature
As Ford went through his attacks on Trump and offered optimism that the Ontario economy could withstand the latest round of tariffs, his political opponents urged him to recall the legislature.

Ontario Premier Says Trump Can “Kiss My Ass” as Trade War Escalates
Ontario Premier Doug Ford made some particularly blunt remarks as Trump continues to threaten tariffs on Canada.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford doesn’t care about President Trump’s threat to increase tariffs on cars and trucks produced in Canada.
On Truth Social Monday morning, Trump wrote that “Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years. Their ridiculously high tariffs on our Farmers and farm products has made life impossible for these great American Patriots, and has long created a 60 Billion Dollar Deficit between our two Countries. Not sustainable, and NOT ANYMORE!
“On January First, 2027, Tariffs on all Cars, Trucks, both large and small, Automotive Parts, and Steel, will be increased to 50%. Build in the U.S. and there are ZERO TARIFFS. Canada will be treated like a State no longer! On Trade, and in other ways, also, they are among the worst Nations in the World to deal with,” Trump continued.
In response, Ford told an Ottawa radio show, “Well, he can kiss my ass as far as I’m concerned. We’re going to go at him full steam, and we buy 400 percent more cars than anyone in the world.”
Ford pointed out that Canada exports oil and gas to the U.S. and supplies some states with electricity, and suggested that “maybe what we should be doing is charging him triple on the oil, triple on the potash, on the uranium, on our metals, and our rare earth metals.”
The Canadian politician, a member of the country’s right-wing Conservative Party, invoked former President Ronald Reagan in his rejoinder to Trump.
“We need to throw everything in the kitchen sink at him. He’s arrogant, he’s cocky, and you know, as Ronald Reagan said, ‘If you come to a draw with a bully, what stops that bully from coming after you the next day and the next day? And that’s all Donald Trump is, is a bully. Well, he’s going to have a rude awakening,” Ford said. He also told the Associated Press that Reagan would be “throwing up” from a picture of him Trump keeps in the Oval Office.
“He’d be throwing up on [Trump] from the picture if he knew what was going on, spinning around in his grave right now,” Ford said. “He should maybe take that picture off the wall and move it somewhere else. Because right now, Ronald Reagan would be disgusted with President Trump.”
Ford has invoked Reagan before in taking shots at Trump, using an audio clip from Reagan in October last year in a TV ad where the former president said tariffs only serve to “hurt every American.” The ad enraged Trump enough to end trade talks with Canada at the time.
Over the weekend, Canada halted tariff negotiations with the U.S. over last-minute demands from Trump such as changing Quebec’s French-language protections and the calculation of tariff payments on Canadian cars, among other details. Ford’s comments, coupled with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s speech to the Canadian people Monday, suggest that the country is not going to back down in this new trade war launched by Trump.

sources.text:
Doug Ford’s increasingly annoyed rhetoric toward Donald Trump reached a new level on Monday when the Ontario premier said the U.S. president could “kiss my ass” in response to his latest tariff threats.
Speaking on a Toronto radio station shortly after Trump posted on social media that he would bring 50 per cent tariffs against Canadian automobiles and auto parts in January, Ford offered the pithy invite about his nether regions, and then said that Canada should “go at him full steam.”
In the same interview, Ford said Canada should use “every tool in our toolbox to go after President Trump” and that “we have to make sure they feel pain.” He said he and his fellow premiers should be willing to impose export tariffs on electricity sent to the United States, and that provinces that send key inputs like oil and potash should be willing to either tariff them or withhold those supplies entirely.
Ford said such a move would cause political blowback for Trump and his Republican Party ahead of midterm elections in November.
“And all of a sudden, you’ll see going into the midterms the reactions when gas jumps one dollar a barrel in the United States,” Ford said.
Prime Minister Mark Carney, while saying bluntly on the weekend that Canada had been “attacked” by its southern neighbour, has so far ruled out restrictions on energy exports as part of Canada’s planned retaliation.
The Ontario premier’s input on Canada-U.S. trade relations has been all over the map in recent days. Long an advocate of harsher retaliation against Trump’s tariff regime, Ford went publicly silent for much of last week while federal negotiators worked on what was said to be a tentative trade deal that would have avoided a new round of Trump tariffs.
It seemed possible then that Ford, who had repeatedly vowed that he would not return U.S. alcohol to the shelves of Ontario’s liquor stores unless Trump removed the tariffs that he began imposing last year, was offside with the prime minister. Ottawa’s tentative deal was said to include reduced U.S. tariffs in exchange for a number of concessions, including an end to provincial alcohol bans.
Ford said on Monday that he was never in favour of such an agreement. “I was dead against this on Wednesday, I was dead against it on Thursday and I’m still dead against (it),” he said during his radio appearance.
Over the weekend it emerged that Ford had sent Carney a letter last Monday outlining the Ontario government’s position ahead of the trade deadline.
“While we share the goal of an agreement that brings relief and certainty to workers and businesses, we must be clear that no deal is better than a bad deal that would only embolden the United States to continue seeking concession after concession,” the letter said.
Ford’s letter said Trump’s threatened tariffs, which have since come into effect, “were clearly intended to gain leverage in negotiations.”
“Canada must remain united and prepared to defend its interests,” the letter said. “We cannot allow arbitrary deadlines, shifting justifications and or escalating tariff threats to weaken our resolve.”
Ford was scheduled to meet with leaders in the Ontario steel industry in Hamilton on Monday morning.
